## Functional Programming - writing reuseable code/functions

ex: rescaling multiple columns to lie between 0 and 1 using 𝑥−min(𝑥)max(𝑥)−min(𝑥)

```{r}
#set up a data frame with random numbers 
df <- tibble(
  a = rnorm(10),
  b = rnorm(10),
  c = rnorm(10),
  d = rnorm(10)
)

head(df)
```

Without using a function, you would manually rescale like this:

```{r}
df <- df |>
  mutate(a = (a - min(a, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(a, na.rm = TRUE) - min(a, na.rm = TRUE))) 

head(df) #now a has numbers not less than 0 and not greater than 1
```

you could copy and paste manually for each column, but that could lead to mistakes :( so instead, you could write a function

Here, this function gives you the value given by that equation:

```{r}
rescale01 <- function(x) {
  value <- (x - min(x, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(x, na.rm = TRUE) - min(x, na.rm = TRUE))
  return(value)
}

df |>
  mutate(
    a = rescale01(a),
    b = rescale01(b),
    c = rescale01(c),
    d = rescale01(d)
  )
```

Even better, you could use mutate(across(Everything function to avoid typing everything out

```{r}
df |>
  mutate(across(everything(), rescale01))
```

## Anatomy of a function

Every function has four key parts:

1.  function name (should be informative but concise)
2.  arguments - function(x) lists the inputs
    1.  multiple arguments could be function(x,y,z)
3.  function body - the {} block containing the actual code
4.  return statement - what the function ends up returning when you run it

### example: converting from fahrenheit to celsius

1.  the conversion formula

    ```{r}
    temp_C <- (temp_F - 32) * 5 / 9
    ```

2.  create the function structure

    ```{r}
    f_to_celsius <- function(temp_F) { #always start with the word function, and the input value/argument
      
      temp_C <- (temp_F - 32) * 5 / 9 #input code from above
      return(temp_C) #add the return statement
    }

    f_to_celsius(2) #test it out! the function should have saved in your environment, and you can input values to make it work 
    ```

Write a function converting Celsius to Kelvin

```{r}
cel_to_kel <- function(cel) {
  kel = cel + 273.15
  return(kel)
}

cel_to_kel(2)
```

### Making plot functions

You can make a function out of a specific plot format to maintain consistency across figures and save time

Use the penguin dataset to create a reuseable plot function

```{r}
library(palmerpenguins)
library(PNWColors)

pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g, y = bill_length_mm, color = island)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
  theme_bw()
```

Name and set up the function:

```{r}
myplot <- function() {
  pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")
  
  ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g, y = bill_length_mm, color = island)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
    theme_bw()
}
```

Add in flexible arguments to the function to make it broadly useable:

```{r}
myplot <- function(data, x, y) {
  pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")
  
  ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y, color = island)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
    theme_bw()
}
```

You need to use {{}} for column names to pass column names as arguments inside formulas, otherwise youʻll get an error:

```{r}
myplot <- function(data, x, y) {
  pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")
  
  ggplot(data, aes(x = {{x}}, y = {{y}}, color = island)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
    theme_bw()
}
```

Then test it

```{r}
myplot(data = penguins, x = body_mass_g, y = bill_length_mm)

#test again!
myplot(data = penguins, x=body_mass_g, y=flipper_length_mm)
```

You could add default arguments so you donʻt have to specify everything: ex like data=penguins

```{r}
myplot <- function(data = penguins, x, y) { #make data=penguins here
  pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")
  
  ggplot(data, aes(x = {{x}}, y = {{y}}, color = island)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
    theme_bw()
}

#now you can call it with just the column arguments, donʻt need to specify the dataset
myplot(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm)
```

### How to layer onto the function

You can use + to add ggplot layers

```{r}
#you can add labels that way to the plot 
myplot(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Flipper length (mm)") 
```

## Adding control flow with if-else

You can make your function even more broad with if-else, aka if you want something in the function or not

### The if-else statement

use if-else to execute different code based on a condition

```{r}
a <- 4
b <- 5

if (a > b) { #if a is greater than b, f will be 20, otherwise it will be 10 
  f <- 20
} else {
  f <- 10
} #all the curlies have to be set up like this apparently spacing wise 

f
```

### Make your function more flexible 

you can add an argument to toggle features on/off - here, you can add a smoother to the plot if argument is true

```{r}
myplot <- function(data = penguins, x, y, lines = TRUE) { #add argument for lines, they are by default on here 
  pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")
  
  if (lines == TRUE) { #if itʻs true, geom-smooth, if not, no geom smooth
    ggplot(data, aes(x = {{x}}, y = {{y}}, color = island)) +
      geom_point() +
      geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
      scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
      theme_bw()
  } else {
    ggplot(data, aes(x = {{x}}, y = {{y}}, color = island)) +
      geom_point() +
      scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
      theme_bw()
  }
}
```

test it out

```{r}
myplot(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm) #here itʻs the default, so there is a smoother 

#without lines
myplot(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm, lines = FALSE)
```
